title: The rally the models barely noticed
body: The S&P 500 closed Friday at 7,297.49, up 1.60% in a shortened Black Friday session that ended at 1 p.m. Eastern, and it capped the strongest week US equities have had in months. The stocks desk responded by moving its composite score from minus 0.252 to minus 0.236. That is the whole of it. The score remains far below the minus 0.10 line at which the desk cuts exposure, so the call is unchanged at Balanced, 50% invested, where it has been since the Nov 23 close. SPY itself finished at 728.73, up 1.7% on the day and 1.8% on the week but still down 5.6% over 21 sessions; QQQ closed at 650.76, up 2.7% on the day and only 0.9% on the week, still 10.3% lower over 21 sessions. A week that felt like a turn barely registered as one.

It is worth seeing where the small improvement actually came from, because it was not broad. Of the six factor groups, five finished the week essentially where they started: internals went from minus 0.550 to minus 0.532, macro from minus 0.210 to minus 0.208, volatility and the calendar group did not move at all. Almost the entire gain sits in the trend group, which improved from minus 0.271 to minus 0.067, and within that group in two readings: SPY against its 200-day average, whose signal went from minus 0.51 to minus 0.16 as price closed within 0.6% of the 733.35 line, and distance from the 52-week high, which went from minus 0.46 to minus 0.12. In other words the index climbed back to a long-term average it had fallen below, and nothing else about the market's condition changed. The largest single positive contributor to the whole composite is not a trend reading at all but equal-weight versus cap-weight, at plus 0.038. Take that one factor out and the score drops to roughly minus 0.27, which is nearly at the minus 0.25 macro gate.

That equal-weight factor is also the most useful thing in the report this week, because it describes the shape of the decline rather than its depth. The internals group reads minus 0.532, which sounds like generalised risk aversion. It is not. The equal-weight S&P has outperformed the cap-weighted index by 4.5% over three months. Semiconductors have underperformed the S&P by 16.1% over the same span. The high-beta basket, measured at the Nov 25 close, is down 27.4% over three months against SPY's 7.1%. An investor looking only at index levels would conclude the market is selling off; the relative moves say something narrower is happening, concentrated in the largest technology companies and in semiconductors specifically. The one genuinely broad warning is in credit, where high yield against Treasuries is down 2.7% over three months and sits in its worst quintile.

The options panel offers a reading that cuts against the obvious interpretation of the week. If the rally had been a relief move into which investors kept their hedges, you would expect put positioning to hold. Instead it unwound into strength. Near SPY's price in the next two monthly expirations, puts per call fell from 2.51 at the Nov 25 close to 1.64 on Friday, with call open interest in that window up 165,678 contracts while put open interest fell 84,592. A dealer gamma flip level reappeared at 760.6, the first time one has shown up in SPY since Nov 18. QQQ's put wall jumped fifty points, from 600 to 650, to sit directly at the money. This is positioning chasing the move rather than insuring against a reversal, and it is context only; it changes no model's exposure and the open interest figures still reflect the prior session's positions.

No US economic data was released on Friday. The number that mattered to the model this week was the third-quarter GDP revision to 4.3% from 3.4%, and it is worth stating plainly that for this portfolio strong economic news is a headwind rather than a tailwind. The revision pushed the 10-year Treasury yield to about 4.91% from 4.86%, and the macro group is the gate that decides whether a negative score means half invested or no equity at all. That group sits at minus 0.208 against a threshold of minus 0.25; higher long yields move it toward confirmation, not away from it. The same move keeps two crash-watch conditions switched on, the 10-year up 0.81 point over six months and the 3-month bill up 0.44 point. A weaker economy would, mechanically, improve this model's reading of the world.

Crash watch finished the week where it began, at Warning with 6 of 10 conditions on, and all three confirmation candidates remain on: under 60% of major risk assets above their 200-day average, that share down 56 points in three months, and the credit proxy in its worst quintile. Those confirmation signals need their caveat said in the same breath every time. They are candidates drawn from a forward test, chosen from 21 conditions tested against 24 warning episodes, which is far more tests than there were events. They are unvalidated and they change no exposure. The chance of a 10% drawdown within six months, measured across the 302 past sessions with a similar score, is 49%.

The concrete level to watch is SPY at 748.85, 2.8% above Friday's close, which is where the stocks desk would flip to Risk On. In the flagship that single crossing is large: SPY would go from 17.5% of the account to 35%, QQQ from 12.5% to 25%, and cash from 45% down to 15%, taking the portfolio from 55% invested to 85%. There is no downside trigger in range at all, which is a consequence of the macro gate rather than of price; while macro sits above minus 0.25 the desk cannot reach Risk Off on price alone, so the realistic near-term path is up to fully invested or nowhere. On the Bitcoin side the level is 74,268, a 23% move from the Nov 25 close of 60,385. That desk is also Balanced, held there by the deep-drawdown rule despite a score of minus 0.304, because Bitcoin is 51.6% below its 2025 high and macro has not confirmed at minus 0.2. High beta remains Risk Off at the Nov 25 close, in Breakdown, 16.6% below its 200-day average.

Ahead, the calendar turns dense after a quiet holiday week. October job openings land Tuesday Dec 1, the November jobs report Friday Dec 4, the Fed decision Wednesday Dec 9 at 2 p.m., and November CPI Thursday Dec 10. Two of those feed the stocks desk directly: the unemployment rate goes into the macro group's labor factor and CPI into its inflation factor, which also governs the re-entry rule that currently requires inflation under 4% and reads 3.7%. The flagship's own live record stands at minus 8.47% since the Oct 26 open against the S&P 500's minus 4.24%, across 24 sessions. Twenty-four sessions is too short to judge, and will remain too short to judge until the record passes 60.
